3. Now let me examine the first point argued by Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant The learned Advocate strenuously argued in support of the proposition that on the elimination of the rent-receiving interest the under raiyati interest of Ayesha Khatun by operation of law became upgraded and attained the independent status of raiyat under the Government. On careful consideration of the argument of the learned Advocate I find it difficult to accept his proposition. Chapter IV of Part IV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 provides for "preparation of record-of-rights." This chapter contains the provision of preparation of record of rights with a view to assessment of compensation regarding interests of all rent-receivers which are liable to be acquired and which have already been acquired under Chapter II of the Act. Section 17 empowers the Government to make an order for preparation of record-of-rights. Section 18 provides that the Revenue-officers are to record certain particulars in the record of rights. Section 19 provides that they are to prepare the draft as well as final publication of such records. Section 20 prescribed the quantum of land 'which can be retained' by a person in his possession. Sections 21 and 22 provide that all lands are subject to payment of fair and equitable rent, as determined by the Revenue-officer in accordance with the provisions of Chapter IV and the rent so determined shall be entered in the record-of-rights. Sections 23 to 28 require the Revenue-officers to assess fair and equitable rents for different classes of tenants. Section 29 provides that the rents entered in the record-of-rights shall be deemed to have been correctly determined and to be fair and equitable.  11. Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, in support of the proposition that the under-raiyati of Ayesha Khatun became upgraded and formed a separate independent bolding, relied upon a decision of this Court in the case of Anwara Begum v. Nurjahan, 27 DLR(AD) 109. From the reported decision it appears that similar question was under consideration on almost similar facts. Two applications under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act were filed in the Court of the Munsif at North Rauzan, Chittagong for pre-emption of transfer of certain land to the preemptee, claiming to be co-sharers in the occupancy raiyati holding to which the said land appertained. The pre-emption cases were contested by the pre-emptee contending, inter alia, that the land sought to be pre-empted appertained to korfa (under-raiyati) holding and as such right of pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was not available to a co-sharer in the raiyati holding. The trial Court on evidence found that the holding was an occupancy raiyati holding and accordingly the pre-emption cases were allowed. On appeal the learned District Judge set aside the judgment and dismissed the pre-emption cases on the finding that the holding was a Korfa (under raiyati) holding without occupancy right and that pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was not available. The learned Single Judge of the High Court however, reversed the decision on taking the view that the Korfa (under raiyati) was upgraded to a raiyati tenancy since14-4-56 as the rent receiving interest of the immediate landlord, this case a raiyat, stood acquired with effect from 14-4-56 under the general notification under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. He allowed the revision cases and restored the judgments of the trial Court. 

 41. Nafisa Khatun by purchasing the 1/3rd share of Akshoy became a co-sharer of Rangubala in the original tenancy but she did not become a co-sharer of Ayesha as Ayesha's interest was an under-raiyati under Rangubala-who was in fact her (Nafisa) co-sharer. This is because, after creating an under raiyati under her Rangubala herself did not become a co-sharer of her tenant, Ayesha, A person who takes lease in respect of a portion of a land of which the other portion is held by the lessor, the former does not become a co-sharer within the meaning of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. This view taken by the learned Single Judge of the then High Court in the case of Manindra Chandra Ghosh V. Mujibul Islam, 12 DLR 785 on which Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed relies is found to be correct for the simple reason that a lessor and his lessee cannot be co-sharers in the same tenancy. The original tenancy, on the creation of the lease stands divided. This was the position in respect of Ayesha Khatun' sunder-raiyat till the acquisition of the rent-receiving interests on "14 April 1956, when Rangubala, along with her superior interests, disappeared from the scene altogether, and consequently, the under-raiyat rose up and became araiyat directly under the Government. This upgrading took place by operation of Jaw) namely, section 3(4)(e) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950. This provides that on the acquisition of rent- receiving interests all tenants holding land in' estates, tenures holdings directly under a rent-receiver become tenants directly under the Government. Effect of this 'upgrading' is same as the merger of interests of a landlord with that of his raiyat under section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act as it stood amended in 1907. Section 22 provides that when the superior landlord purchases an occupancy-holding under him, the holding itself disappears and consequently the status of an under-raiyat is raised to that of a raiyat. The logic behind this merger is that when a landlord purchases a raiyat holding in execution of a rent decree he shall hold the land not as a raiyat but as a land-lord such as a proprietor or tenure-holder, and the under-raiyati created by the outgoing raiyat not being annulled at the option of the landlord the under raiyat takes the position of the raiyat. In the instant case, after disappearance of all classes of rent receivers, only one class of tenants remained in the field paying rent directly to the Government. In the instant case Ayesha Khatun became a tenant directly under the Government with effect from 15-4-1956. It is true that Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 came into operation on a much later date. 1962, but during this intervening period, only one class of tenants remained on the land paying rent direct to the government. Retention of different classes of tenants in the record of rights, prepared or revised under Chapter IV of this Act, was intended for completing some consequential work such as realization of arrears of rent at different rates existing at the time of the acquisition, payment of rent to the government at the existing rates, payment of compensation tothe ex-rent-receivers. During this period payment of rent to any person other than government as well as sub-letting of land was totally prohibited. As such, retention of the former classification of tenants in record of rights did not stand in the way of automatic creation of only one class of tenants. In the case of "Mobasher Ali v. Mokbul Hossain;" 19 DLR, 271 a Division Bench of the High Court, on examining all previous decisions on this point took a similar view which was approved and confirmed by the Appellate Division in the case of Anwara Begum Vs. Nurjahan, 27 DLR (AD) 109. Again, in the instant case, the date of upgrading of the under-raiyati into a raiyati is not material. As such, I see no ground to take a different view about the date of the statutory upgrading of the status of under-raiyats.
